result:
At dawn the city looked as if someone had rinsed it overnight. Roofs shone darkly, windows held pale squares of sky, and the street smelled of stone and coffee. I carried no umbrella, only a paper bag containing two pears and a book whose pages had begun to loosen from its spine. At the corner, a bus sighed open and swallowed three sleepy passengers. One wore a bright yellow scarf that made the gray morning seem briefly theatrical. I kept walking, listening to water tick against awnings and gather in the cracks between paving stones. Somewhere, a baker lifted a metal shutter.

Warm bread breathed into the street, and a small dog tugged its owner toward the smell with urgent conviction. I thought of all the plans I had made for the day, each one neatly folded like a map. Rain blurred their ink. Perhaps this was useful. Perhaps a day could be allowed to arrive without instructions.

At the park gate, a girl in red boots jumped into a puddle and laughed when the water leaped back. Her father pretended to be shocked, then jumped too. For a moment, neither seemed to care about wet cuffs or waiting trains. I passed them slowly, feeling the paper bag soften against my coat.

At home, I would set the pears on the table and open the book beside them. Maybe its loose pages would fall free; maybe I would read one aloud while the kettle warmed. Outside, the rain continued, patient.
